title: Bayway Refining Co. v. Oxygenated Marketing & Trading A.G.
summary: The buyer failed to establish that an additional tax-allocation clause materially altered this merchant contract.
notes:
Court: Second Circuit (2000).

The opinion reports New York treatment of arbitration as per se material while rejecting the analogy to this limited tax term. That is not a nationwide holding about arbitration. The notes’ Union Carbide case concerns later-assessed back taxes and states a different view of hardship. The 60,000-barrel quantity and tax figure were checked on printed p. 285’s image.

sections.Parties: Bayway, the seller, sought reimbursement from Oxygenated Marketing & Trading (OMT), the buyer, for tax on their petroleum-product sale.
sections.Material Facts: OMT faxed an offer to buy 60,000 barrels of MTBE. Bayway accepted with an additional clause allocating sale-related taxes to the buyer. Its acceptance was not expressly conditional. OMT did not object and accepted delivery. Bayway paid $464,035.12 in tax and invoiced that amount. OMT disputed the clause’s incorporation.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment for Bayway. The Second Circuit affirmed, including the allocation of the burden of proving material alteration and admission of industry-practice evidence.
sections.Issue: Who bears the burden under § 2-207(2)(b), and did this tax clause produce the requisite surprise or hardship?
sections.Holding: The party resisting the additional term bears the burden of proving material alteration. OMT failed to raise a genuine factual issue. The court expressly left undecided whether hardship independently establishes material alteration.
sections.Reasoning: Both parties were merchants, and the claim invoked the material-alteration exception to incorporation. The clause concerned a discrete sale rather than an open-ended indemnity. Subjective surprise was insufficient without objective surprise to a reasonable merchant. Unrebutted trade evidence established that buyers customarily bore these taxes: three sample forms said so expressly, one incorporated tax into price, and a silent form did not negate the practice. OMT could avoid the tax by registration, reinforcing the allocation. Even assuming hardship were an independent test, thin margins and an unaffordable loss did not establish it here; the liability was limited, customary, and avoidable.

sections.Parties: Bayway was the petroleum seller; OMT was the buyer.
sections.Material Facts: Bayway’s acceptance incorporated a tax-allocation clause by reference. OMT accepted delivery. Bayway paid $464,035.12 in excise tax because OMT lacked registration for exemption, then sought reimbursement.
sections.Procedural History: The Southern District of New York granted Bayway summary judgment. The Second Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: Did the added tax clause materially alter the merchants’ contract under New York UCC § 2-207(2)(b)?
sections.Holding: OMT bore the burden of proving material alteration and failed to raise a genuine factual dispute.
sections.Reasoning: Unrebutted industry practice defeated objective surprise. OMT’s hardship showing was insufficient; the court left open whether hardship independently establishes material alteration. The court also upheld consideration of reply-stage evidence.
